message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Happy to help, and being slightly terrified is a good sign: it means you'll take care. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it.** You can feel it as a little ridge underfoot, and it catches the light.

It matters especially with your 30 × 60 cm tiles, because long tiles are often very slightly bowed. Two ways to keep it down:

- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets. They're well worth it for a first floor.
- **If you lay the tiles in a staggered (brick) pattern, offset each row by no more than a third of a tile**, rather than by half. This stops the high middle of one tile meeting the low end of the next. Check the tile box, because many manufacturers specify this.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for **a mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. Avoid white or very light grey on a floor: they show dirt within weeks. A mid-grey hides everyday grime and still looks neat against pale tiles.

Two extras help:

- **Keep the joints narrow.** 2–3 mm suits rectified porcelain.
- **Use a stain-resistant grout,** or seal a standard cement grout once it has cured. If you want the lowest-maintenance option, epoxy grout barely stains at all, but it's trickier to work with.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tile the whole floor first, then fit the toilet on top. You avoid fiddly cuts around the pan, the floor underneath is fully waterproofed, and if you ever replace the toilet there won't be an untiled patch. Before you start, check that the toilet's waste connection will still line up once the floor is raised by the thickness of the tile and adhesive.

## How many boxes to buy

| Step | Calculation |
|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m = **4.32 m²** |
| Area of one tile | 0.30 m × 0.60 m = **0.18 m²** |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles** |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 = 26.4 → **27 tiles** |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4 → **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes would give you exactly 24 tiles, with no room for a single cut or breakage. The extra tiles in the fourth box are useful to have: keep any you don't use for future repairs. When you buy, check that all the boxes have the **same batch number**, because the shade can vary slightly between batches.

## Message for the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for the bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise for a few hours. We'll aim to keep it to a reasonable time and get it done as quickly as we can.
>
> Thank you as well for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks. We really appreciate it, and it should be gone soon!
>
> [Your names]

If you can, add the hours, for example "between about 9 and 12". People mind noise much less when they know when it'll stop.

## Three tips for a first-time floor tiler

1. **Get the floor ready first.** The base needs to be solid, flat, clean and not bouncy. If it's a timber floor, it usually needs plywood or tile backer boards screwed down over it first. Most failed floors fail here, not in the tiling itself.

2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix anything.** Set out a row of loose tiles, with spacers, in both directions to plan where the cuts will fall. Adjust the layout so you don't end up with thin slivers of tile at the doorway or along a visible wall. Then mark your starting lines on the floor.

3. **Get full adhesive coverage under each tile.** With large tiles, spread adhesive on the floor using the right notched trowel *and* butter a thin layer on the back of each tile. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the back is almost fully covered. Hollow spots crack later. Mix small batches of adhesive so they don't start setting before you use them.

The videos do make it look effortless, and it will take you longer than it takes them. That's completely normal. Work slowly, check often, and it'll come out well. Good luck!
